weather.headline: Extreme Heat Warning issued July 27 at 7:55PM MST until July 29 at 8:00PM MST by NWS Phoenix AZ
weather.description:
* WHAT...Dangerously hot conditions. Afternoon temperatures 110 to
116 degrees. Major Heat Risk.

* WHERE...In Arizona, Parker Valley and Yuma. In California, Imperial
Valley, and Palo Verde Valley.

* WHEN...Until 8 PM MST /8 PM PDT/ Wednesday.

* IMPACTS...Heat related illnesses increase significantly during
extreme heat events. Overexposure can cause heat cramps and heat
exhaustion to develop and, without intervention, can lead to heat
stroke.
weather.instruction:
An Extreme Heat Warning means that a period of very hot temperatures,
even by local standards, will occur. Actions should be taken to
lessen the impact of the extreme heat.

Take extra precautions if you work or spend time outside. When
possible, reschedule strenuous activities to early morning or
evening. Know the signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion and heat
stroke. Wear lightweight and loose-fitting clothing when possible and
drink plenty of water.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Public cooling shelters are available in some areas. Consult county
officials for more details.
weather.areaDesc: Parker Valley; Yuma; Imperial Valley; Palo Verde Valley; Chuckwalla Valley

weather.instruction:

alcohol and caffeine. Stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of

fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

unattended vehicles for even a moment. Car interiors will very
quickly reach lethal temperatures.

events.title: Flood Watch
events.description: * WHAT...Flash flooding caused by excessive rainfall is possible. * WHERE...Portions of central New York, including the following county, Sullivan and northeast Pennsylvania, including the following county, Pike. * WHEN...From Tuesday morning through Wednesday evening. * IMPACTS...Excessive runoff may result in flooding of rivers, creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations. Creeks and streams may rise out of their banks. Flooding may occur in poor drainage and urban areas. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS... - Multiple rounds of showers and storms are expected to move over the area starting late tomorrow morning through Wednesday. Rainfall rates could exceed 1-2 inches per hour with the heaviest downpours. Even though this area has been somewhat dry recently, multiple rounds of heavy downpours could cause urban flash flooding and/or small streams and creeks to flow out of their banks. Two day rainfall totals are expected to be in the 2-3 inch range, with 3-6 inches possible in portions of the Catskills if upslope enhancement matches up with storms producing heavy downpours. - http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood

illnesses.
weather.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

events.title: Flood Watch
events.description: * WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall is possible. * WHERE...Hampden, Hampshire and Franklin Counties in western Massachusetts, as well as Hartford and Tolland Counties in Northern Connecticut. * WHEN...From Tuesday afternoon through Wednesday evening. * IMPACTS...Excessive runoff may result in flooding of rivers, creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations. Creeks and streams may rise out of their banks. Flooding may occur in poor drainage and urban areas. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS... - Moderate to heavy rainfall is expected to develop Tuesday afternoon into Wednesday across the Watch area. The heaviest rainfall is expected Tuesday evening into Wednesday. Excessive rainfall rates are possible, which could trigger instances of street flooding and contribute to rises on rivers, streams and larger river basins. Two to three inches of rain are expected in the Watch area, with locally higher amounts possible especially along the eastern slopes of the Berkshires and portions of western Hartford County. - http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood

location.region: Hartford; Tolland; Western Franklin; Eastern Franklin; Western Hampshire; Western Hampden; Eastern Hampshire; Eastern Hampden

Olean, moving east at 30 mph.

HAZARD...Wind gusts up to 50 mph and half inch hail.

unsecured objects. Minor hail damage to vegetation is
possible.

Shinglehouse, Eldred, Oswayo, and Ceres.
weather.instruction:

roadways.

shelter inside a building or vehicle.

this storm passes.

weather.headline: Beach Hazards Statement issued July 27 at 9:38PM PDT until July 29 at 6:00PM PDT by NWS Eureka CA
weather.description:
* WHAT...Increased threat of sneaker waves expected.

* WHERE...Southwestern Humboldt and Coastal Mendocino Counties.

* WHEN...Through Wednesday afternoon. .

* IMPACTS...Large, unexpected waves can sweep across the beach
without warning, sweeping people into the sea from rocks,
jetties, and beaches. These sneaker waves can also move large
objects such as logs, crushing anyone caught underneath.
weather.instruction:
Don't be fooled by an ocean that looks calm.  There can be
30 minutes of small waves before a sneaker wave strikes.  Avoid
rocks and jetties. Avoid steep beaches.  Stay much farther back
from the water and never turn your back on the ocean.

weather.description:
SMWTAE

The National Weather Service in Tallahassee has issued a

* Special Marine Warning for...
Coastal Waters From  Ochlockonee River to Apalachicola FL out to 20
Nm...
Coastal Waters from Mexico Beach to Apalachicola out 20 NM...
Coastal waters from  Suwannee River to Keaton Beach out 20 NM...

Waters from Suwannee River to Apalachicola FL from 20 to 60 NM...

* Until 200 AM EDT/100 AM CDT/.

* At 1237 AM EDT/1137 PM CDT/, a severe thunderstorm capable of
producing waterspouts was located 10 nm south of V Tower, moving
southeast at 20 knots.

HAZARD...Waterspouts and wind gusts 34 knots or greater.

SOURCE...Radar indicated.

IMPACT...Waterspouts can quickly form and capsize boats...damage
vessels...and create suddenly higher waves. Make sure all
on board are in a secure location and wearing life
jackets. Expect wind gusts in excess of 34
knots...suddenly higher waves...frequent lightning...and
heavy downpours. Make sure all on board are wearing life
jackets.

* Locations impacted include...
S Tower, C Tower, and V Tower.
weather.instruction:
Move to safe harbor immediately as gusty winds and high waves are
expected.

Thunderstorms can produce sudden waterspouts. Waterspouts can easily
overturn boats and create locally hazardous seas. Seek safe harbor
immediately.

weather.headline: Extreme Heat Warning issued July 27 at 11:32PM CDT until July 28 at 7:00PM CDT by NWS Paducah KY
weather.description:
* WHAT...Dangerously hot conditions with heat index values up to 111.

* WHERE...Caldwell and Christian Counties.

* WHEN...Until 7 PM CDT Tuesday.

* IMPACTS...Heat related illnesses increase significantly during
extreme heat and high humidity events.
weather.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

events.description: * WHAT...For the Beach Hazards Statement, 3-6 feet with sets to 7 feet expected. For the Coastal Flood Advisory, minor coastal flooding expected. For the Coastal Flood Advisory, from 5 PM Wednesday to 3 AM PDT Saturday. For the High Surf Advisory, from 5 PM Wednesday to 5 PM PDT Saturday. * IMPACTS...Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only isolated road closures expected. Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions and localized beach erosion. Breaking waves can sweep people off jetties and docks, and into dangerous seas. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS...A long period southerly swell of 3 feet at 17 seconds continues through Wednesday. A higher amplitude swell associated with Hurricane Genevieve of around 5 feet at 14 seconds builds late Wednesday into Thursday. Swell and associated surf look to subside late Saturday into Sunday.

events.title: Air Quality Alert
events.description: The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment has issued the following... WHAT...Ozone Action Day Alert. WHERE...Douglas, Jefferson, Denver, western Arapahoe, western Adams, Broomfield, Boulder, Larimer, and Weld Counties WHEN...400 PM Monday July 27 to 1200 AM Tuesday July 28 IMPACTS...Ozone Action Day Alert is now in effect for the Front Range Urban Corridor. Ozone concentrations in the Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups category are possible Monday afternoon and evening, mainly within and near the Denver metro area. Lower ozone in the Moderate category is expected for Tuesday. For Colorado air quality conditions, forecasts, and advisories, visit: https://www.colorado.gov/airquality/colorado_summary.aspx If possible, please help us reduce ozone pollution by limiting driving gas and diesel-powered vehicles until midnight, Monday night, July 27, 2026. Colorado is also addressing ozone pollution through state policies. For more information about health impacts and how ozone pollution forms in Colorado, visit: https://cdphe.colorado.gov/ozone- pollution-and-your-health HEALTH INFORMATION...Increasing likelihood of respiratory symptoms and breathing discomfort in active children and adults and people with lung disease, such as asthma. Active children and adults, and people with lung disease, such as asthma, should reduce prolonged or heavy outdoor exertion Monday afternoon and evening.

location.region: Larimer, CO; Douglas, CO; Weld, CO; Boulder, CO; Broomfield, CO; Jefferson, CO; Arapahoe, CO; Adams, CO; Denver, CO

events.title: Flood Watch
events.description: * WHAT...Flash flooding caused by excessive rainfall is possible. * WHERE...A portion of Southeast Arizona, including the following areas, Baboquivari Mountains, Dragoon and Mule and Huachuca and Santa Rita Mountains, Upper San Pedro River Valley and Upper Santa Cruz River Valley/Altar Valley. * WHEN...Until 5 AM MST Tuesday. * IMPACTS...Excessive runoff may result in flooding of rivers, creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS... - An organized cluster of storms or mesoscale convective system (MCS) in northeast Sonora Mexico is expected to slowly drift northwest across portions of south-central Arizona late this evening and overnight tonight. This storm system will be capable of producing moderate rainfall with pockets of very heavy rainfall. Although widespread rainfall amounts between 0.50 and 1.00 inches are anticipated, localized rainfall amounts between 1 and 3 inches will be possible resulting in localized flash flooding. The heaviest rainfall is expected over the southwest half of Santa Cruz county and extreme south-central Pima county and may have significant impact on the Nogales Wash overnight. Heavy rainfall Monday evening along Highway 286 and along and Arivaca Road have made portions of south central Pima county vulnerable to flash flooding with additional rainfall overnight. - http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood

weather.description:
* WHAT...Heat index values up to 110 expected.

* WHERE...Portions of south central and southwest Alabama and
southeast Mississippi.

* WHEN...From 10 AM to 9 PM CDT Tuesday.

* IMPACTS...Hot temperatures and high humidity may cause heat
illnesses.
weather.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

In Missouri, Jefferson MO County. * WHEN...Until 7 PM CDT Tuesday. * IMPACTS...Heat related illnesses increase significantly during extreme heat and high humidity events.

location.region: St. Clair; Monroe; Jefferson

weather.headline: Extreme Heat Warning issued July 27 at 9:10PM CDT until July 28 at 7:00PM CDT by NWS St Louis MO
weather.description:
* WHAT...Dangerously hot conditions with heat index values up to 106.

* WHERE...In Illinois, Monroe IL and Saint Clair IL Counties. In
Missouri, Jefferson MO County.

* WHEN...Until 7 PM CDT Tuesday.

* IMPACTS...Heat related illnesses increase significantly during
extreme heat and high humidity events.
weather.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors. Young children and
pets should never be left unattended in vehicles under any
circumstances. Take extra precautions if you work or spend time
outside. When possible reschedule strenuous activities to early
morning or evening. Know the signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion
and heat stroke. Wear lightweight and loose fitting clothing when
possible. To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety
and Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks
in shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.
weather.areaDesc: St. Clair; Monroe; Jefferson

events.title: Flood Advisory
events.description: Rainfall this afternoon of up around 3 inches has lead to a rapid rise in the South Fork on the Republican River. Rapid in bank rises are occurring. * WHAT...Small stream flooding caused by excessive rainfall is expected. * WHERE...Along the South Fork on the Republican River in West Central Cheyenne County in northwestern Kansas... * WHEN...Until 300 AM CDT Tuesday. * IMPACTS...Minor flooding in low-lying and poor drainage areas. Dangerous flows over low-water crossings. River or stream flows are elevated. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS... - At 839 PM CDT, the public reported heavy rain in the advisory area due to thunderstorms. This will cause small stream flooding. Rapid river rises will cause minor flooding in the advisory area. Between 1 and 3 inches of rain have fallen. Additional rain is possible later tonight. - Some locations that will experience flooding include... St. Francis.

location.region: Cheyenne, KS

weather.headline: Flood Advisory issued July 27 at 8:46PM CDT until July 28 at 3:00AM CDT by NWS Goodland KS
weather.description:
Rainfall this afternoon of up around 3 inches has lead to a rapid
rise in the South Fork on the Republican River. Rapid in bank rises
are occurring.

* WHAT...Small stream flooding caused by excessive rainfall is
expected.

* WHERE...Along the South Fork on the Republican River in West
Central Cheyenne County in northwestern Kansas...

* WHEN...Until 300 AM CDT Tuesday.

* IMPACTS...Minor flooding in low-lying and poor drainage areas.
Dangerous flows over low-water crossings. River or stream flows are
elevated.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- At 839 PM CDT, the public reported heavy rain in the advisory
area due to thunderstorms. This will cause small stream flooding.
Rapid river rises will cause minor flooding in the advisory area.
Between 1 and 3 inches of rain have fallen. Additional rain is
possible later tonight.
- Some locations that will experience flooding include...
St. Francis.
weather.instruction:
Turn around, don't drown when encountering flooded roads. Most flood
deaths occur in vehicles.

Be especially cautious at night when it is harder to recognize the
dangers of flooding.

Please report observed flooding to local emergency services or law
enforcement and request they pass this information to the National
Weather Service when you can do so safely.

* WHEN...From 10 AM to 9 PM CDT Tuesday.

* IMPACTS...Heat related illnesses increase significantly during
extreme heat and high humidity events.
weather.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

Do not leave young children and pets in unattended vehicles. Car
interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Stay cool, stay hydrated, stay informed.

* IMPACTS...Heat related illnesses increase significantly during

weather.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

Do not leave young children and pets in unattended vehicles. Car
interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

Stay cool, stay hydrated, stay informed.

events.title: Air Quality Alert
events.description: The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment has issued the following... WHAT...Ozone Action Day Alert. WHERE...Douglas, Jefferson, Denver, western Arapahoe, western Adams, Broomfield, Boulder, Larimer, and Weld Counties WHEN...400 PM Monday July 27 to 1200 AM Tuesday July 28 IMPACTS...Ozone Action Day Alert is now in effect for the Front Range Urban Corridor. Ozone concentrations in the Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups category are possible Monday afternoon and evening, mainly within and near the Denver metro area. Lower ozone in the Moderate category is expected for Tuesday. For Colorado air quality conditions, forecasts, and advisories, visit: https://www.colorado.gov/airquality/colorado_summary.aspx If possible, please help us reduce ozone pollution by limiting driving gas and diesel-powered vehicles until midnight, Monday night, July 27, 2026. Colorado is also addressing ozone pollution through state policies. For more information about health impacts and how ozone pollution forms in Colorado, visit: https://cdphe.colorado.gov/ozone- pollution-and-your-health HEALTH INFORMATION...Increasing likelihood of respiratory symptoms and breathing discomfort in active children and adults and people with lung disease, such as asthma. Active children and adults, and people with lung disease, such as asthma, should reduce prolonged or heavy outdoor exertion Monday afternoon and evening.

events.title: Special Weather Statement
events.description: Daytime temperatures will reach 70 to 75 degrees later this week, and will be hottest on Wednesday and Thursday. Temperatures this warm, and for this long, happen about once per year. The long duration of warmer days may impact subsistence activities like berry picking, fishing, and hunting. This could also affect people who are extremely sensitive to heat (like elders or infants), especially if they are unable to cool down or stay hydrated. Actions: Keep homes cool by closing curtains during the day and opening windows at night. If outdoors, stay hydrated and dress in lighter and looser clothing. Be alert to signs of heat stress in yourself and others.

events.description: Oregon Department of Environmental Quality has issued an Air Quality Advisory until noon PDT Wednesday. For additional information...please visit the Web site at http://www.oregon.gov/DEQ

events.title: Beach Hazards Statement
events.description: * WHAT...For the Beach Hazards Statement, dangerous rip currents and breaking waves due to elevated surf. For the Coastal Flood Advisory, minor coastal flooding expected. For the High Surf Advisory, large breaking waves of 4 to 8 feet with dangerous rip currents, highest across south facing beaches exposed to southerly swells. * WHERE...Catalina and Santa Barbara Islands. * WHEN...For the Beach Hazards Statement, through Wednesday afternoon. For the Coastal Flood Advisory, from 5 PM Wednesday to 3 AM PDT Saturday. For the High Surf Advisory, from 5 PM Wednesday to 5 PM PDT Saturday. * IMPACTS...Flooding of sea water is likely around the time of high tide, over vulnerable low-lying coastal areas such as parking lots, beaches, and walkways. Significant damage to roads or structures is NOT expected. There is an increased risk for ocean drowning. Rip currents can pull swimmers and surfers out to sea. Large breaking waves can cause injury, wash people off beaches and rocks, and capsize small boats near shore. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS...High tides of 6.2 to near 7.0 feet will occur in the evening hours through Friday night, peaking tonight through Thursday night. In conjunction with the highest expected surf from the Hurricane Genevieve southerly swell, the best potential for minor coastal flooding impacts is expected Wednesday and Thursday evening.

weather.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out
of the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors. Young
children and pets should never be left unattended in vehicles
under any circumstances.

Take extra precautions if you work or spend time outside. When
possible reschedule strenuous activities to early morning or
evening. Know the signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion and heat
stroke. Wear lightweight and loose fitting clothing when
possible. To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational
Safety and Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent
rest breaks in shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone
overcome by heat should be moved to a cool and shaded location.
Heat stroke is an emergency! Call 9 1 1.

weather.instruction:
This warning is reserved for only the hottest days of the year and is
issued when temperatures are expected to rise to dangerous levels.

Day hikers on Bright Angel Trail should descend no farther than 1 1/2
miles from the upper trailhead. Between the hours of 10 AM and 4 PM,
hikers should be out of the canyon or at Havasupai Gardens or Bright
Angel campgrounds, physical activity is discouraged. All hikers
should have adequate gear, including a wide-brimmed hat, sunscreen,
salty snacks, sufficient water, and electrolyte mix. Doubling your
calorie intake helps maintain your energy.

Hike smart.

weather.instruction:

weather.instruction:
Do not leave young children and pets in unattended vehicles. Car
interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Take extra precautions if you work or spend time outside. When
possible, reschedule strenuous activities to early morning or
evening. Know the signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion and heat
stroke. Wear lightweight and loose fitting clothing when possible and
drink plenty of water.

weather.headline: Extreme Heat Warning issued July 27 at 10:49PM MST until July 30 at 11:00AM MST by NWS Phoenix AZ
weather.description:
* WHAT...Dangerously hot conditions. Afternoon temperatures 110 to
116 degrees. Major Heat Risk.

* WHERE...In Arizona, Parker Valley and Yuma. In California, Imperial
Valley, and Palo Verde Valley.

* WHEN...Until 11 AM MST /11 AM PDT/ Thursday.

* IMPACTS...Heat related illnesses increase significantly during
extreme heat events. Overexposure can cause heat cramps and heat
exhaustion to develop and, without intervention, can lead to heat
stroke.
weather.instruction:
An Extreme Heat Warning means that a period of very hot temperatures,
even by local standards, will occur. Actions should be taken to
lessen the impact of the extreme heat.

Take extra precautions if you work or spend time outside. When
possible, reschedule strenuous activities to early morning or
evening. Know the signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion and heat
stroke. Wear lightweight and loose-fitting clothing when possible and
drink plenty of water.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Public cooling shelters are available in some areas. Consult county
officials for more details.
